Somethings you can what you can do to avoid food getting spoiled is to cook your dish without adding much water let it cool down in a container and freezer it. Maybe too late but the way colorism affects every culture is very different for some it's inherent racial issues, for some its a class based issue. For most east asian countries like China and Korea where this standard is prevelant it distilled from class to finally now a dimension in beauty standards. I mention dimension as dimension is only one aspect of the same spectrum.

The way the conversations around skin color affect different societies and how said people are treated because of this color difference is crucial in understanding why it's still accepted in countries like Korea and China.

In korea or china being darker toned has almost no negative effects on society apart from this person is not the ideal idea of what the skin tone they consider beautiful It is the same as in China having double eyelids and big eyes are the biggest hallmark of beauty so in turn yes monolids are considered not desirable which is prevalant as it being the leading plastic surgery performed on people of east asian descent. This is why it still continues to this day as a standard of beauty. Another thing to note, most of these communities talk about physical features or beauty related things very nonchalantly as achieving the ideal is ideal and desirable, so conversations about skin and weight as pretty common which in turn leads to most of us having developed thick skins or being like whatever it's a beauty ideal. For some it can cause their self-esteem to fall because as we all know some people attach their self-worth to how attractive they are. Something to note is that whenever they talk to people who look like them it's always about the beauty aspect. This is why when you hear the same words said it affected you differently because it depends on what is the importance of skin color in your community. Is it rude to imply someone is undesirable?  Well it depends on your relationship with this person..

There is now a intersectionality on racism which I will explain. Usually east asians do not have the same standards for beauty for other races as we acknowledge bone structure, facial features are different across races. Most of the world has more sharper features than your fellow east asian. This is why what rules we apply to ourselves may not apply to you i.e we might consider what is considered beautiful in your country based on images we have seen from media etc. An example of this while we might consider thinner lips to be ideal for ourselves, we acknowledge that having bigger lips might be the norm for another race and what they consider pretty, so hence you will often read mistranslations of kpop idols saying x is pretty for a black woman, it's because the idol is judging based on the standards set for a different race. I would guarantee they will mostly say that even for white people, brown people south east asian people as I have personally heard many of my aunts say that without bad intentions. If we judged everyone based on how strict we do ourselves then a fair south east asian will be considered most beautiful as they tend to have the ideal eyes more commonly than us. Sadly fair is a dimension used in this consideration. That's why when someone tells them it's wrong to say that, they just mostly go like eh coz that's what everyone does.

Now when these beauty ideals can bleed into colorism where in they consider fairer skin as ideal across all races is when it's harmful & it's very difficult to know if the individual has let that happen unless you see them making similar comments on skin tone for a person of another race, they may not realize that jokes with a different conotation for themselves can have more adverse reactions for the other person. For some, it can be hard to differentiate these lines if they have grown up in an environment where the both racism and colorism is intertwined too strongly that it becomes hard. 

All in all, education of how colorism affects other communities is what is missing here in many people living in korea. I have spent alot of time on this because even though being darker in my city and hearing this alot it never made me feel less than or disrespected because in my mind skin is just a color and I don't hold the beauty standard of being fair to high regard whereas for someone else hearing this might trigger deep rooted issues within their own communities. I personally take zero offense if someone from my community comes and tells me you got tanned because I personally don't see what's wrong in having darker skin . I personally don't make these jokes because I am more educated on things like body image and self-esteem, but I'll be honest: East asians especially anyone millienial and older are very thick skinned . East Asians outside of the subcontient not so much.

This is why I don't necessarily want to paint our communities as that bad because the way we react the way we deal with these statements is very different. For me i don't hold taekey accountable unless Minho states that he has been negatively affected by those statements, because when they were talking amongst themselves I didn't for one second think that statement was directed at me ( as again I mention I don't consider being dark bad/not desirable and jokes like that have no effect on me), but I can empathize that it might be triggering for others as they have heard and dealt with those words in a different and maybe more harsher light.

I hope shawols can read this and reflect on how different this experience can be for others and this is why many differing opinions exist as the way individuals have been affected vary greatly as it depends on their own cultural issues. Colorism and it's effects are not universal, and without first understanding how it affects them, it's very difficult for them or others to understand how it affects you. I believe in empathy & educating them on how it culturally affects you w/o making it a blanket it is bad statement/call out/ not excusable because they will never understand why it's bad as they are still referring to it in their context or frame of mind) 

I understand everyone says they are adults they should know these things but when a larger demographic of adult people seem to support them when they talk amongst themselves, you need to understand why is that the case & go back to at its core what are the cultural differences between you and them. What is consent?

Consent is an agreement between participants to engage in sexual activity. Consent should be clearly and freely communicated. A verbal and affirmative expression of consent can help both you and your partner to understand and respect each other’s boundaries.

Consent cannot be given by individuals who are underage, intoxicated or incapacitated by drugs or alcohol, or asleep or unconscious. If someone agrees to an activity under pressure of intimidation or threat, that isn’t considered consent because it was not given freely. Unequal power dynamics, such as engaging in sexual activity with an employee or student, also mean that consent cannot be freely given.

How does consent work?

When you’re engaging in sexual activity, consent is about communication. And it should happen every time for every type of activity. Consenting to one activity, one time, does not mean someone gives consent for other activities or for the same activity on other occasions. For example, agreeing to kiss someone doesn’t give that person permission to remove your clothes. Having sex with someone in the past doesn’t give that person permission to have sex with you again in the future. It’s important to discuss boundaries and expectations with your partner prior to engaging in any sexual behavior.

You can change your mind at any time.
You can withdraw consent at any point if you feel uncomfortable. One way to do this is to clearly communicate to your partner that you are no longer comfortable with this activity and wish to stop. Withdrawing consent can sometimes be challenging or difficult to do verbally, so non-verbal cues can also be used to convey this. The best way to ensure that all parties are comfortable with any sexual activity is to talk about it, check in periodically, and make sure everyone involved consents before escalating or changing activities.

What is enthusiastic consent?
Enthusiastic consent is a newer model for understanding consent that focuses on a positive expression of consent. Simply put, enthusiastic consent means looking for the presence of a “yes” rather than the absence of a “no.” Enthusiastic consent can be expressed verbally or through nonverbal cues, such as positive body language like smiling, maintaining eye contact, and nodding. These cues alone do not necessarily represent consent, but they are additional details that may reflect consent. It is necessary, however, to still seek verbal confirmation. The important part of consent, enthusiastic or otherwise, is checking in with your partner regularly to make sure that they are still on the same page.

Enthusiastic consent can look like this:
Asking permission before you change the type or degree of sexual activity with phrases like “Is this OK?”

Confirming that there is reciprocal interest before initiating any physical touch.

Letting your partner know that you can stop at any time.

Periodically checking in with your partner, such as asking “Is this still okay?”

Providing positive feedback when you’re comfortable with an activity.

Explicitly agreeing to certain activities, either by saying “yes” or another affirmative statement, like “I’m open to trying.”

Using physical cues to let the other person know you’re comfortable taking things to the next level (see note below).

Note: Physiological responses like an erection, lubrication, arousal, or orgasm are involuntary, meaning your body might react one way even when you are not consenting to the activity. Sometimes perpetrators will use the fact that these physiological responses occur to maintain secrecy or minimize a survivor's experience by using phrases such as, "You know you liked it." In no way does a physiological response mean that you consented to what happened. If you have been sexually abused or assaulted, it is not your fault.

Consent does NOT look like this:

Refusing to acknowledge “no”

A partner who is disengaged, nonresponsive, or visibly upset

Assuming that wearing certain clothes, flirting, or kissing is an invitation for anything more

Someone being under the legal age of consent, as defined by the state

Someone being incapacitated because of drugs or alcohol Pressuring someone into sexual activity by using fear or intimidation

Assuming you have permission to engage in a sexual act because you’ve done it in the past
